Beyond Eleven Minutes: Maria's Search for the Body, Love, and God

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-10-31

I finished the book with a strange picture in my head. Three people sit in one room and none of them speaks. One thinks about the body, one about love, one about God. All three live inside the same young woman, yet they refuse to meet. Most of us arrange our lives the same way. The body goes in one room, love in another, and God on the highest shelf, where the dust of ordinary life cannot reach. We worry that if the three touch, something will spoil. In Eleven Minutes, Paulo Coelho opens the doors between those rooms. He does not claim that body, love and spirit are the same thing. He only shows what it costs a person to keep them apart inside herself.

Maria is a girl from a small town in Brazil. Her parents are not rich, and she works in a draper’s shop. No great catastrophe happens to her, and nobody drags her anywhere. Girls like her can be found in a back lane of Dhaka, a neighbourhood in Chattogram, a small town in Sylhet. I think Coelho kept her past plain on purpose. Had it been dramatic, we would have said she had no choice and moved on. An ordinary girl with ordinary wishes who still ends up on this road turns the question back toward us.

As a child Maria invents love stories about boys at school. Early heartbreak teaches her that love means pain and dependence, so she decides to keep her hands on the wheel of her own life. Love can wait. Money and independence come first. It sounds small, but much of the rest of the book rests on that decision.

On a holiday in Rio she meets a Swiss man who offers her a contract as a dancer in a Geneva nightclub. To Maria, Europe is the door out of her little town. What she finds in Geneva is a cold politeness, a language she cannot speak and faces that do not know her. Everything is there and none of it is hers. At the Copacabana club she begins to work as a companion to the customers, and her only friend is Nyah, a Filipina woman.

Here I had to change my own first impression. I used to think Maria slid into prostitution through a string of small compromises. In the book she does not slide. She makes a decision and draws up a plan: a limited time of this work, money saved, a farm bought back in Brazil for her parents and herself, and then the wait for real love. That calculating quality is what unsettled me most. When a young woman must do the arithmetic of survival so coldly, we should ask how few other options stood behind the sum, and we rarely want to look.

The title number sits right there on the cover. Coelho tells us the act itself takes about eleven minutes. Set against the hatred, curiosity and condemnation society piles around those minutes, the figure is almost absurd. But Maria’s diary shows that the weight lies elsewhere, before and after. It lies in the doubt in front of the mirror, in the way a client’s eyes show no trace of who she is, in the lonely hour when she goes home and feels around for her own self-respect. The diary entries that close each chapter are what turn her from a character into a person.

Between shifts Maria goes to the library, where she reads about sex and also about running a farm. I love that detail, two kinds of books in one pair of hands. She also learns to tell her clients apart. Some are cruel, some come to drown a grief, some come because they are alone. She realises that sex often tells a story of loneliness more than of appetite. I should say that Coelho imagines a woman’s inner life from the outside, yet these observations ring honest.

Two men then enter her life. One is Terence, an Englishman from the music business who flies into Geneva for one particular reason. Through him Coelho takes up pain and pleasure, control and surrender. Maria is frightened, but she is more curious than afraid. In my reading, the point of this section is the power to decide. Where to stop, what to accept, what to refuse: all of it is hers to say. The body is neither a market item nor a shame to be hidden. Learning her own limits and respecting herself inside them seems to be Coelho’s real subject here.

The other man is Ralf Hart, a twenty-nine-year-old Swiss painter, famous and wealthy. One day he walks into the club, looks at Maria and tells her there is a light inside her that he wants to paint. Ralf is tired himself and has lost interest in sex. Maria first writes him off as one more desperate man among millions. Three days later he returns and pays for a whole evening, and they go to his house, talk, and exchange symbolic gifts. Perhaps for the first time, someone gives her time and listens. Then her old fear returns. Does love mean becoming weak again? By now she has only about ninety days left before her planned departure. What I like in this relationship is how little it demands and how much attention it pays. Ralf does not want to give her a new name. He wants to see the person who is already there.

Which brings me back to the three rooms. The boldest thing about Eleven Minutes, to my mind, is that it seats body, love and spirit at one table. We have been taught to keep them apart: the body behind shame, love in the house of dreams, God at the place of worship. They are like three countries with no visa between them. Coelho waves people across without papers. As I read it, the book says a person can sell her body and still stay honest with herself, can face her own questions, and can even find her own way to God. That collides head-on with the morality most of us inherited, and the novel draws its strength from the collision.

Even so, Coelho does not hand the reader an easy answer. When I closed the book a kind of weariness stayed with me, because neither our usual contempt nor our usual pity fits. You have to listen before you judge and look at the person before you name her. What happens to Maria in the end, whether she goes home as planned or Ralf changes her mind, I will leave alone. Those who have not read it deserve to find out for themselves.

I do have an objection. A rich, famous and handsome artist is a little too convenient for Maria’s love story. In places the philosophising runs so long that the story stalls. The book is far from flawless, but the questions it raises are not trivial ones.

For readers in Bangladesh the novel carries a different kind of question. Every day many Marias leave home, from Dhaka lanes, the port areas of Chattogram, the tea gardens of Sylhet. Abroad they become domestic workers in Dubai or factory hands in Malaysia, and at home they become garment workers and nurses. Some chose their road, and some were pushed down a dark one. We read about them in the newspaper and see their numbers in NGO reports, but we never read their diaries. Coelho’s book is an attempt to peek into one of those unread diaries. It neither condemns the trade nor romanticises it. It shows how poverty, dreams, mistakes, courage and the silence of everyone around her can add up to a road.

So the book cannot be set down in comfort. A few questions stay behind. When we call someone bad too easily, how much of her story belongs to our own society, our economy and our double standards? Do I think of my own body as something forbidden, or as something I am responsible for? And the God I speak of: is he only a keeper of accounts for sin and virtue, or a silent witness who stays beside me through every mistake, break and recovery? These questions are uncomfortable, but that discomfort is more alive than any easy, questionless peace. After the last page, it still feels as though the night has not ended.
